title: With Due Respect (Vol. 1) -- Ch. 9: Dress Her Down Anyway
keywords: capable of repetition yet evading review
primary_topics: Chapter 9 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 1) -- CJP's December 13, 2009 Inquirer column arguing that PP 1959, declaring martial law and suspending the writ of habeas corpus in Maguindanao, was 'so inane and so baseless that even a law student will readily disown it,' and that the Supreme Court should strike it down even though GMA had just 'lifted' it

Why PP 1959 was patently unconstitutional: the 1987 Charter allows martial law only for 'invasion or rebellion' (actual, not 'looming' or 'brewing') when 'public safety requires' it, and the Ampatuan-clan massacre of 57 people -- however unpardonable -- was not 'rebellion' under RA 6968, since it was not a public rising in arms to deprive the government of its powers

His reading of GMA's motive: that the belated martial-law edict was an attempt 'to test her hold on Congress and, more important, on the Supreme Court' -- the killings being 'plain murder' solvable by 'normal police powers'

The mootness rebuttal anchored in David v. Arroyo: that lifting PP 1959 to dodge a 'judicial dressing down' should not moot the petitions, because the violation is grave and 'capable of repetition yet evading review' -- so the Court 'should not tire of firmly striking down the trifling of civil liberties'
sub_topics: The thesis: PP 1959 (dated December 4, 2009), declaring 'a state of martial law' and suspending the writ of habeas corpus in Maguindanao, was so 'inane' that even GMA's lifting of it should not deter the Court from 'chastising the government for recklessly violating our Charter'

Patently unconstitutional: the 1987 Constitution provides 'only two grounds' for martial law -- 'invasion or rebellion' -- and even then requires proof that 'the public safety requires' it; 'looming' or 'brewing' rebellion is not enough -- it must be 'actual and real'

Not rebellion: PP 1959 cited the alleged 'rebellion' of the Ampatuan clan accused of massacring 57 people, but the massacre 'does not constitute rebellion' under RA 6968, which defines rebellion as 'rising publicly and taking arms against the Government... to deprive the Chief Executive or the Legislature... of any of their powers'

The common-sense refutation: the Ampatuans could not be 'rising against the government' when they controlled the entire province (the governorship and most mayoralties), when GMA had 'always been their close political ally and generous patron,' and when the province's two congressmen 'belong to the clan'

The real motive: the killings were 'plain murder' solvable by 'normal police powers,' so the belated martial law was, in CJP's view, an attempt by GMA to 'test her hold on Congress, and more important, on the Supreme Court' -- Congress being expected to close ranks on the partisan 'numbers game'
The mootness gambit: with petitions lodged in the Court, the Palace lifted PP 1959 'before the Court could act,' hoping the petitions would be dismissed as 'moot and academic'

The David v. Arroyo precedent: just three years earlier the Court refused to dismiss the petitions against PP 1017 despite its lifting, because the violation was grave and 'capable of repetition yet evading review' -- 'there is no guarantee that PP 1017, or one similar to it, may not again be issued' -- and struck it down 'to prevent future constitutional aberrations'

The warning and the close: an emboldened President could mask 'feigned or real' terrorist attacks or 'automated election glitches' as excuses for 'iron rule again and again'; reprising his David v. Arroyo opinion ('playing with fire... burn down the country'; the condemnation of 'legal hocus pocus' like the moot-and-academic theory), he urges that the Court 'should not tire of firmly striking down the trifling of civil liberties'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 9 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 1), CJP's December 13, 2009 Inquirer column, argues that Presidential Proclamation 1959 -- declaring 'a state of martial law' and suspending the writ of habeas corpus in Maguindanao -- was 'so inane and so baseless that even a law student will readily disown it,' and that the Supreme Court should strike it down even though GMA had just 'lifted' it. It was patently unconstitutional, he writes, because the 1987 Charter permits martial law only for 'invasion or rebellion' -- actual, not 'looming' or 'brewing' -- when 'public safety requires' it, and the Ampatuan-clan massacre of 57 people, however unpardonable, was not 'rebellion' under RA 6968, which requires 'rising publicly and taking arms against the Government... to deprive' it of its powers. The 'rebellion' theory collapses on common sense, he says: the Ampatuans controlled the entire province (the governorship, most mayoralties, both congressmen) and were GMA's 'close political ally and generous patron,' so they had nothing to rise against -- the killings were 'plain murder' solvable by 'normal police powers.' In CJP's reading, the belated edict was an attempt to 'test her hold on Congress, and more important, on the Supreme Court,' and lifting it before the Court could act was a bid to dodge a 'judicial dressing down' by having the petitions dismissed as 'moot and academic.' But, he argues, the petitions should not be dismissed: three years earlier, in David v. Arroyo, the Court refused to let the lifting of PP 1017 evade review because the violation was grave and 'capable of repetition yet evading review,' striking it down 'to prevent future constitutional aberrations.' Warning that an emboldened President could mask 'feigned or real' attacks or 'automated election glitches' as excuses for 'iron rule again and again,' he reprises his David v. Arroyo opinion ('playing with fire... burn down the country'; the condemnation of 'legal hocus pocus' like the moot-and-academic theory) and urges that the Court 'should not tire of firmly striking down the trifling of civil liberties.'
